Take three things and leave the rest: (a) the calibration round — re-judge September's committed corpus with the coded panel and require it to reproduce the recorded verdicts before any new round is believed, £7.50, and if it fails nothing after it means anything; (b) the 'four counters that count the wrong thing' as a step-2 prerequisite, especially the bars count, since a warm database silently voids the price layer and would make every round after the first measure a different product; (c) the one-page note on what can actually stop a run, written before any acceptance criterion names a refusal. Refuse the four measurement rounds and the £190 ceiling: two rounds, and everything after the first conditional on it.

4. MOVE THE KILL-CHECK EARLIER AND PUT IT ON AZN. Replace the spine's M1-at-45-sessions with document-first's step-7 steer: one AZN run at ~£10.50 after the keyhole, the reconciliation and the anchor land (~25 sessions), on the one subject where this thesis has already been half-tested and failed. Pre-register the reading three ways as that plan does. Reject journey-first's mid-point alternative — re-rendering a stored run under new code judges a document the platform would never emit.

MEASUREMENT, assembled: document-first's pre-registration discipline (September value beside every threshold, committed at a hash predating the first paid run, anti-gaming clause, and view_stated explicitly excluded because azn2 already scored it 3/3) + measurement-first's calibration, mutation corpus and discriminating pair + the spine's verifiability-first bar. Harden one thing all four got soft: do not let 'equal' carry the headline brief threshold. State it as 'platform named on better_answers_the_brief in ≥3 of 6, with equal reported separately', so a round of six equals cannot be read as a win. And carry the azn A/B swap into the harness as a regression test, or the new round will be compared against a baseline that is wrong by 17 votes.

EFFORT: the honest composite is ~55 sessions and ~£45 to the kill-check, with the reach and prose work conditional on it. That is document-first's budget discipline applied to the spine's ordering, with the bank and the journey pulled forward where the evidence puts them.

gaps.what: No story about which report is current, and the plans all depend on one. `start_run`'s own docstring says it outright (src/aer/services/runs.py:78-84): "One report per request, not one job... a second run of a request that already produced a report needs a story about which report is current, and there is not one yet." So a refresh of an already-researched company is a NEW REQUEST producing a SECOND REPORT, with nothing marking the first superseded. No diagnosis item and no plan names this.
gaps.whyItMatters: It silently undermines four separate things every plan builds. (1) The refresh journey is audit use case 2, rated "yes, once fixed" — but what is fixed is the UUID leak, not the identity question. (2) Three plans write the operator's stated view onto a report via `theses.report_id`; two reports on the same company means two standing views and no rule about which one holds. (3) `history.prior_digest_for` feeds "the prior view" into the next run's planner (planner.py:319) — with no supersession it will feed whichever report `latest_report` happens to return. (4) Every plan's re-measurement round commissions MSFT twice and calls the second "the refresh case"; if it is the same request `start_run` returns the existing job and nothing runs, and if it is a new request the round is measuring an orphan. `decisions.py` and `theses` both already implement supersede-with-a-reason; reports do not.
gaps.suggestedItem: Decide and record what a second report on a company means: a `superseded_by` column on `reports` written at the moment a later run for the same company is approved, with the operator told at the final gate that they are superseding a report dated X and carrying view Y; `latest_report`, the company history page, the Obsidian export and `prior_digest_for` all read the un-superseded one. Needs an ADR — it is the missing half of ADR 0090's "a resumed run is the same job" and it gates the view work in every plan.

gaps.what: An entire second half of the product is undiagnosed, and three plans wire the operator's view straight into it without looking. `src/aer/services/` holds thesis_monitor.py, decisions.py, portfolio.py, post_trade.py, risk.py, performance.py, watchlist.py, listings.py, splits.py, knowledge.py and lessons.py, with web templates for portfolio, watchlist, monitor, decisions, risk, theses and knowledge, under ADRs 0073-0085, 0093-0094 and 0102-0107. Not one of the ninety findings and not one workstream in four plans touches any of it.
gaps.whyItMatters: Every plan stores the operator's stated view through `services/theses.py` as an ADR 0102 judgement. `thesis_monitor.py`'s own docstring says a monitor pass reads each premise that carries a predicate, resolves the metric, measures it from fiscal years filed since, and — on a `contradicted` status — OPENS THE THESIS GATE. So the plans are creating the first real production writes into a monitoring loop nobody has examined, whose findings can gate something, and whose premises need testable predicates or a review date that the prefilled-from-`what_would_change_the_view` design does not produce. It is also the single largest untested claim about "user-ready": the operator is a private investor with a book, and the audit tested only the research half.
gaps.suggestedItem: Before any view work lands, spend one session reading thesis_monitor.py, theses.py and decisions.py end to end and answer three questions in writing: does a thesis prefilled from `investment_thesis` produce premises the monitor can actually read (predicate or review date), what does a `contradicted` finding do to an operator who never asked for a monitor, and is the book/watchlist subsystem in scope for "user-ready" at all. Then either scope it in with its own workstream or state in the non-goals paragraph that it is out — but do not write into it blind.

gaps.what: Use case 12, "Living with it", is the least-covered row in the audit's own matrix and no plan owns it. The audit rates it "partly" and says explicitly "the Windows path is untested here (§9)". Meanwhile `aer backup`, `aer verify-backup`, `aer restore`, `aer gc-artefacts` and `services/retention.py` exist and are careful (backup.py's docstring: "A backup that has never been read is not a backup"), and no plan runs any of them once.
gaps.whyItMatters: Invariant 1 says every externally derived fact traces to a hashed artefact. That guarantee lives in `var/artefacts/` plus Postgres on one laptop. If the store is lost, five reports and every future one become unverifiable, and the platform's single unqualified win evaporates. Three plans are about to make this worse by copying verified excerpts into immutable exported reports — increasing what depends on the store while nobody has proved it restorable. Windows is a harder gap: the whole stack is docker-compose, Postgres, Redis, a worker terminal and WeasyPrint's native dependencies, and if the operator's machine is Windows the audit establishes nothing about whether any of the journey fixes are even reachable. Two plans mention WeasyPrint-on-Windows as a stalled operator move; none makes bring-up or recovery a deliverable.
gaps.suggestedItem: A short "living with it" workstream, half a session: run `aer backup` then `aer verify-backup` then `aer restore` into a scratch database once and record the result in docs/developers/testing-by-hand.md; measure the artefact store's growth per run and state whether `gc-artefacts` needs a schedule; and run one full journey on the operator's actual machine, Windows or not, before the re-measurement round rather than after.

gaps.what: `excluded_sources` is a form field the operator fills in, echoed back on the request detail page as if it were a rule, and enforced by a prompt. Grep across src/ returns exactly one consumer: `agents/planner.py:277-280`, which lists the domains in the planner's user turn. The request schema validates them, the DB stores them, the detail template renders them, and no fetcher, no `_established_host` and no tier check ever reads them.
gaps.whyItMatters: It is a broken promise on the one page where the operator states what the run may not read, and it is the exact failure mode the diagnosis already flags as a caution buried inside the IR allow-list item — but nobody files it as its own defect. Two plans then propose an operator-supplied domain ALLOW-list read by `_established_host` and `SafeFetcher`; shipping an allow-list enforced in code beside a deny-list enforced in a prompt is an incoherent pair, and the deny-list is the half the operator has already been using. It also sits next to invariant 8's principle that authorisation is enforced in code, not by prompt text.
gaps.suggestedItem: Read `excluded_sources` in the fetcher and in `_established_host` alongside whatever allow-list lands, refuse a matching host with a recorded reason, and add a test that a domain the operator excluded cannot be fetched even when a model composes its URL. An hour, no ADR, and it should ship in the same commit as the allow-list or the pair contradicts itself.

gaps.what: Every plan adds at least one new blocking refusal — cross-section figure agreement, "refuse FINAL while any disagreement is escalated", the answers-block emitter refusing an uncited entry, the claim-level figure guards — and not one gives the operator a recorded-reason override. This is a failure mode the plans would introduce, not one they inherit.
gaps.whyItMatters: The repository already decided this shape for the identical case: ADR 0018 requires a per-citation override with a mandatory written reason and explicitly forbids a bulk one, precisely because an unverified citation with no recovery leaves the run lost. A deterministic figure index over a 14,000-word document with 831 calculations will find near-misses — a rounded figure in prose, the same number printed in millions in one section and billions in another, a figure the reconciliation pass matches by name that is genuinely two different things. When it is wrong, the operator has a £7 run that cannot be approved and no page that will let them say so. That is a brand-new dead end created by ISSUE-2 work, and it would land straight into the dead-end inventory the ISSUE-1 workstreams are trying to empty. Only plan 1 mitigates, and only by reporting before refusing.
gaps.suggestedItem: A single rule applied to every new blocking check: it may refuse, and the operator may override one instance with a mandatory written reason that is recorded and rendered on the document, exactly as ADR 0018 already specifies for citations. Build it once, beside the gate's refusal path, and require every new check to route through it. Add each new check to the dead-end inventory as a row that must have an exit before the check goes blocking.

gaps.what: Printing verified excerpts into the exported report creates a path from untrusted fetched bytes, through an immutable artefact, into the NEXT run's planner prompt — and no plan mentions it. Three plans note the licence conflict with `aer purge-licensed`; none notes the injection one.
gaps.whyItMatters: Invariant 8 says untrusted content is data, never instruction, and is enforced by wrapping and labelling at the point a model sees it. An excerpt from a T5 page or an untagged EX-99 press release printed verbatim into report.md is no longer wrapped — it is the platform's own prose. `history.prior_digest_for` then feeds the prior report's content forward into the planner (`agents/planner.py:319`), and the Obsidian export puts it in a vault the operator may paste anywhere. The evidence-reach workstreams make this materially worse by admitting worker-fetched pages and raising the tier ceiling, so the two changes compound in a direction nobody traced. The extract step already flags injection signals (`services/injection.py`; msft2's worker log records `extract.flagged` with `invisible_styling` on the exhibits), and `decide_quarantine` keys on publication date and tier, not on those signals.
gaps.suggestedItem: Before excerpts are printed: decide what an excerpt is when it leaves the trusted boundary. Minimum — excerpts print only for tiers whose licence permits it AND whose source carries no injection signal; the prior-research digest carries figures and section titles and never another report's excerpt prose; and a test asserts an injection-flagged document's excerpt never reaches an exported artefact. One paragraph in the export ADR, and it costs nothing if decided now rather than after.

gaps.what: Nobody checks whether the valuation is any good, and all four plans make it more prominent. The audit's §9 lists "whether the valuation a run produces is right rather than traceable" as unestablished. msft1's own DCF returns $242.78 (Gordon growth) and $449.79 (exit multiple); azn2 returns $333.48 and $169.80 — a 96% spread. Every plan treats this as a labelling problem (name the method, name the period, pick the base) rather than as a signal.
gaps.whyItMatters: The programme's arc is: make the valuation visible to the writers, anchor it to a market capitalisation, put an implied upside beside it, state a view over it, and put all of that on the front page and in the one-pager. If the model underneath is producing a band whose ends differ by a factor of two on operator-confirmed assumptions, the plans convert a traceable-but-uninformative number into a prominent-and-decisive one — and the platform's whole defence is that it never states a figure it cannot defend. A judge who notices that the two terminal methods disagree by 96% and the front page shows one of them will discount the view harder than they discounted the silence.
gaps.suggestedItem: One offline session before the view work: take the five stored runs' recorded valuation inputs and outputs and write down what the spread between terminal methods is on each, what drives it, and whether the platform should print a band rather than a point (the valuation section already calls the gap "the honest width of the answer"). Make it an explicit operator decision — does the front page carry a point, a band, or neither — and add a check that refuses to designate a base case when the two methods diverge past a stated threshold, rather than picking whichever row was written last.

gaps.what: The operator's own time is never budgeted, and runs cannot be parallelised. `src/aer/worker.py:245` records the rule: "One run at a time. A second concurrent run would double the rate against every data source". A measurement round of three runs is therefore three sequential ~35-minute machine runs plus six or seven gate sittings each, against gate pages totalling 26,392-34,540 words. All four plans budget pounds and sessions; none budgets hours of the operator's attention.
gaps.whyItMatters: Plan 3 schedules four measurement events; plan 4 two; plans 1 and 2 two each including a steer. Each round is realistically a full day of the operator's attention, not an afternoon — and that is the same operator who must also take twelve decision points, read four ADR drafts and walk §4.4's six by-hand checks. The audit itself notes "the audit's own stops added hours and are not the product's", so the cost is invisible in every number the plans quote. This is the constraint most likely to make a good plan stall halfway.
gaps.suggestedItem: Put an operator-hours column beside the sessions and pounds in the running order, priced from the audit's own gate-page word counts and the 30-40 minutes of attention it records per run. Then make the gate-reduction work (the financials page cut, the standing assumptions, the composed sitting) a prerequisite of the FIRST measurement round rather than a later tranche — it is the only item that reduces the cost of measuring everything else.

gaps.what: The skills system — invariant 7's entire subject — is undiagnosed and unused as a lever. `src/aer/skills/` (execution, frontmatter, library, resolution, examples), `services/skill_authoring.py`, `services/skill_dry_run.py`, a `templates/skills/` web surface and ADR 0108 all exist. Nothing in ninety findings or four plans establishes whether an operator can write a methodology skill, whether it works, or whether it is usable.
gaps.whyItMatters: Two reasons. First, invariant 7 ("skill files are additive-only... enforced structurally, not by prompt text") is one of eight non-negotiables and is the only one with no test in any plan beyond a containment assertion that `rating` stays reserved. Second, and more interesting for ISSUE 2: a standing house methodology that composes into every run is something a console session structurally cannot carry between notes. The judges preferred the console for reaching a conclusion; the platform's answer to "why is this better the tenth time" is partly the operator's own accumulated method, and no plan proposes using it.
gaps.suggestedItem: Half a session of triage: write one real methodology skill as the operator would (there is an example at `src/aer/skills/examples/bear_case_in_one_page.md`), run it through `skill_dry_run`, and record whether the authoring surface is usable and whether the additive-only guarantee holds against a skill that tries to relax something. If it works, it belongs in the ISSUE-2 argument; if it does not, invariant 7 has no live evidence behind it and that should be said.

gaps.what: There is no path to correct or retract an approved report. `decisions.py` supersedes a decision with a reason and withdraws the old one; `theses` carry withdrawal-with-reason; `retention.py` purges a payload with a mandatory stated reason. `reports` have none of this — the row is written at render and is thereafter a fact.
gaps.whyItMatters: Every plan increases the number of operator-supplied and operator-approved figures reaching a shareable artefact: a stated view, a settled challenge, an overridden citation, an amended classification, a hand-typed assumption. Each is a place the operator can later discover they were wrong. Today the only remedies are to run the company again (which, per gap 1, produces a second report with no story about which is current) or to leave a wrong document standing. For a tool whose entire proposition is an auditable record, having no recorded way to say "this report is wrong and here is why" is a hole in the record itself.
gaps.suggestedItem: Fold this into the supersession ADR from gap 1: a report may be marked withdrawn or corrected by the operator with a mandatory reason, appended to the audit chain with the report as subject, rendered on every surface that lists it, and carried into the prior-research comparison — the same shape `decisions.py` and `theses` already use. The schema work is one column and one append-only table; the decision is whether the exported artefact itself must carry the mark, which it should.

wrongAssumptions: That a single-shot blind read of one document can measure what this platform is for. Every structural advantage the platform has — replay, the refresh against a prior view, a record that survives the run, an operator's standing thesis, a second and tenth report on the same company — is invisible in a one-document comparison against a console note. All four plans adopt the audit's instrument unchanged and pre-register targets inside it. The operator's own framing invites that, but nobody says the honest thing: on single-shot quality the platform may draw at best indefinitely, and the axis where it wins has never been measured once. A second measurement — the same brief run twice, three months apart, judged on whether the second document is better for having the first — costs one extra run and is the only test the console cannot sit for.

That agreement with the filing means the figures are right. "0 contradicted of 779 checkable figures" measures whether a printed numeral matches a filed one. It says nothing about whether the DCF, the WACC, the terminal method, the beta or the residual-income fade is defensible — the audit's §9 lists exactly that as unestablished. All four plans treat the valuation as a delivery problem and none proposes checking it, while every one of them makes it more prominent.

That the September console notes are a fixed bar. They are one model's output at one date. The plans reuse them for rounds landing months later and report only the news-staleness asymmetry. A platform that reaches parity with September's console in January has not reached parity with January's console, and the plans' own no-regression floors contain nothing that would notice.

That effort estimates compose across ninety interdependent findings, and that ADRs are free. The plans name between 14 and 25 new or amended ADRs, several of which gate work that cannot start without them, and none schedules ADR writing as its own effort. In this repository an ADR is a substantial document that must argue against named prior decisions; at half a session to a session each that is 10-25 sessions nobody has counted.

That the eighteen-section institutional spine is the right product for one private investor. All four plans take the spine as given and add a nineteenth section to it. Quick mode already exists, drops nine sections, scales budgets to 0.6, and has never been run, costed or judged — and the judges skimmed the platform's documents faster per thousand words than the console's. Whether the right answer is a six-section note that answers the brief is the largest untested product question on the board and no plan asks it.

That a "shareable report" has a reader other than the operator. Use case 9 is rated partly and three plans spend five to nine sessions making the exported file checkable by someone who does not have the interface. That reader may not exist: this is a single-operator local tool, and the audit's own strongest result (use case 10) is explicitly "yes, IN THE INTERFACE". If the only reader is the operator, the export work is worth less than the interface work and the priority inverts.

That the judges' decisive-field prose is causal. It is post-hoc rationalisation by a model asked to justify a choice it has already made. Four plans build their entire ordering on which phrases appear in it, and the one experiment that tested causation directly — azn2, which fixed the valuation and stated a view and changed nothing — is the evidence against reading it that way.
sequencingObjections: Plan 2 commissions a live M&T run at step 4, two steps before the evidence-cap fix at step 6. That £8 buys the first bank report ever produced and it will carry every contradiction defect the programme exists to remove — an Executive Summary denying a valuation the front page prints, unresolved escalated challenges, an unlabelled per-share figure. Either move the keystone port ahead of the bank run, or accept that step 4 proves only that the pipeline completes and say so.

All four plans gate several steps on the ADR 0030 licence answer and none has a fallback if it takes weeks or needs the vendor. This is the operator re-reading an executed agreement, possibly with a question to EODHD; it is not a decision they can take in a sitting. Name a default that lets work continue — build the derived figures behind a policy flag that is off until the answer arrives, so the code lands and only the render switch waits.

New blocking checks land before the measurement rounds in three of four plans, and only plan 1 gates them advisory-first. A cross-section figure check, a FINAL refusal on unsettled challenges and an answers-block emitter refusal are three new ways a round's own runs can strand — in a programme whose measurement depends on runs completing, and on a platform where three of six September runs did not. Every new refusal should report for two live runs before it blocks, and should be on the dead-end inventory with an exit before it does.

Refusing FINAL while any disagreement is escalated ADDS up to eight mandatory operator decisions at gate 3, in the same programme where the journey workstreams are removing decisions and cutting a 13,592-word gate page. No plan reconciles the two. Sequence the adversarial adjudication and the materiality gate BEFORE the compulsion, so most challenges are settled by code and the operator is handed two rather than eight.

The declared gap field must precede the self_consistency_of_absence metric — the metric is only sound as a structural intersection over declared absences, not as a phrase list. Plans 1 and 3 catch this; plans 2 and 4 leave the metric ahead of or alongside the field. Fix the order or the metric ships lexical and is wrong.

The re-measurement rounds assume runs can be commissioned together. `worker.py:245` says one at a time by design, so a three-run round is sequential in machine time and serial in the operator's attention. Schedule rounds as two days of operator time, not an afternoon, and put the gate-reduction items ahead of the FIRST round rather than after it — they are the only work that makes measuring everything else cheaper.

Nobody proves the artefact store is restorable before it becomes load-bearing for printed excerpts. `aer verify-backup` and `aer restore` exist and have never been exercised in any plan. Run them once, early — it is half a session — because from the moment excerpts are printed into immutable reports, the store holds the only copy of what a reader can check.

The view work is scheduled before anyone has looked at `thesis_monitor.py`, which reads exactly the rows the view writes and can open a gate off them. Put one session of monitor triage in front of the view item in every plan, or the first operator-stated thesis is the first production write into an unexamined loop.
cheapestWinsMissed: A deterministic run-to-run figure diff for a refreshed company. Both runs' calculation and fact rows are stored; a table showing what moved since the prior report — revenue, margins, the valuation, the WACC, and which filings are new — is pure Python over rows the platform already holds. It is the actual payload of the refresh use case, it needs no model call and no ADR, and it is the one thing a console session structurally cannot do because it has no prior run to diff against. Every plan fixes the Prior Research Comparison's blanks; none proposes the comparison a reader actually wants.

Enforce `excluded_sources` in code. It is a request-form field, validated, stored and rendered back to the operator, and its only consumer in src/ is `agents/planner.py:277-280` — a line in a prompt. One predicate in the fetcher and in `_established_host`, plus a test that a model-composed URL on an excluded domain is refused. An hour, and it closes a broken promise on the page where the operator states what the run may not read.

Run `aer backup`, `aer verify-backup` and `aer restore` once, against a real database and store, and write the result into docs/developers/testing-by-hand.md. Half a session. Every claim the platform makes about traceability rests on an artefact store whose recovery path has never been exercised, and three plans are about to increase what depends on it.

Print the evidence window on the front page: the newest filing read, its date, the as-of date, and one line naming what a reader should know is not in the record (no interims for this filer, no peer financials, no guidance located). Deterministic, composed from the run's own source documents, and it answers the staleness complaint that appears in five of nine decisive fields even on runs where the staleness cannot be fixed. Honest disclosure is cheaper than new reach and the judges rewarded it elsewhere — two of them called the book-weight caveat the strongest paragraph in the document.

The operator reads two documents blind themselves, once, for £0. The audit's §4.4 checks 1 and 2 already specify it, the files are committed, and the operator is the actual decision-maker whose answer the three model judges are standing in for. Four plans build a judging harness before anyone asks the person whose money is at stake to spend ninety minutes on the two documents that already exist.

One quick-mode run, £4. `AnalysisMode.QUICK` is implemented in data, drops nine of eighteen sections and scales budgets to 0.6, and has never been run, costed or judged. It is the cheapest possible test of the largest unasked product question — whether the eighteen-section spine is the right shape — and three plans mention it in passing while one refuses it outright.

A `superseded_by` mark on reports with a recorded reason. `decisions.py` and `theses` both already implement supersede-and-withdraw-with-a-reason; copying that shape to reports is one column, one append-only row and a render line. It closes the "which report is current" hole, gives the operator a way to say a report was wrong, and is a prerequisite of the refresh journey and the stated view that every plan schedules without it.

gaps.what: No plan asks the judges what would change their answer, and no plan re-judges with the interface available — so eighteen expensive reads produced complaints but no ordering over the backlog, and all four plans are guessing at the ordering.
gaps.whyItMatters: The rubric (judges/reads.json, read keys: subject/doc/lens/path/rubric/identity; rubric keys: focus_questions, checklist, view_stated, view_argued_not_recited, bear_case_in_the_body, numbers_explained, verifiability, still_to_look_up, would_act_on_it, first_thing_to_check, reading_minutes, strongest_paragraph, weakest_paragraph, overall) has no key asking what single change would move would_act_on_it off 'no'. So the plans infer priority from which complaint appears most often in prose — which is why all four rank 'the view' first despite azn2 having a view. Separately, all 18 reads used report.md while §4.1 concludes 'the platform's verifiability advantage lives in the interface, not in the document it exports' and §4.4 check 3 asks the operator to walk three figures in the interface. Nobody has tested whether the advantage converts when a judge can reach it. WS3-equivalents in all four plans (5–7 sessions each) rest on that untested conversion.
gaps.suggestedItem: Before any code: add two rubric keys — 'what one change to A would move you off no' and 'what would you need to see to prefer A' — and re-run the existing 18 reads over the existing documents at judge-token cost only. In the same pass, run three extra reads of msft1 with the run console reachable, to establish whether the provenance advantage converts when it is not confined to the file. Both are free of live runs and both would reorder the backlog before ~40 sessions are committed to a guessed order.

gaps.what: No plan holds the operator-confirmed assumptions fixed across a measurement round, and three of four commission MSFT twice inside the round.
gaps.whyItMatters: §3.1 measures exactly this: two MSFT runs one UTC day apart, same filings, 837 calculation rows compared — 178 keys identical, 18 keys differing across 527 rows — and 'every differing key is downstream of exactly three inputs', of which the decisive one is 'one model-proposed assumption the operator confirmed — the exit multiple, 14× against 15×'. Value per share moved $512.50 → $485.29, 5.6%. The audit's own conclusion: 'the arithmetic is reproducible and the *report* is not, because one of its inputs is a model's opinion confirmed at a gate.' A judged round whose headline per-share figure is 5.6% adrift between two runs of the same subject is measuring the operator's confirmations alongside the code, and no plan's protocol says which assumption set the round uses.
gaps.suggestedItem: Record the confirmed assumption set (risk-free rate, ERP, beta, tax rate, exit multiple, terminal growth) in the pre-registration document as fixed values, and have the round's runs confirm those exact values at the assumptions gate. State in the protocol that a round in which an assumption differs from the pre-registered set is reported with that difference named. This costs nothing and is the difference between a measurement and a re-roll.

gaps.what: No plan buys a current-model console baseline; all four make the fresh baseline contingent on the platform winning, which is backwards.
gaps.whyItMatters: The comparator is one API call with three constants: audit/baseline/anthropic_baseline.py sets MODEL='claude-opus-5', EFFORT='high', MAX_TOKENS=48_000, 25 searches. The repository's own price table already carries `claude-fable-5-1` annotated 'The tier above Opus, which the provider already accepts as a route' (src/aer/providers/costs.py, DEFAULT_PRICES). So a tier above the baseline's model is already routable, today, before a session is spent. All four plans then reuse the September notes for two to four rounds across four to five months on the argument that a stale note is 'a lower bound on the console'. That holds for recency and fails for reasoning: better_argued, better_answers_the_brief and better_on_the_focus_questions are model-quality dimensions, and the model has moved. A platform win at the final round against a four-month-old, one-tier-down comparator is not a win, and the contingency runs the wrong way — a *win* is what needs re-testing, not a loss.
gaps.suggestedItem: Make one fresh baseline on the current best route a required line in the final round's budget (~£8–11 at the AZN rate), not an option purchased only on a win. Pin the baseline's model and effort in the protocol and record them; §9 already flags that 'the console itself' is not established and reads.json records no model for the judges either. Report every comparison as 'platform-at-date-X against baseline-at-model-Y' or the two rounds are not comparable in the direction that matters.

gaps.what: No plan separates the composed half of the view from the operator-authored half, so the round cannot attribute the movement — and the operator authors a field blind judges then score.
gaps.whyItMatters: All four plans recommend the operator states the view at the final gate, stored as an ADR 0102 judgement. Two problems the plans do not name. First, attribution: a run carrying both a composed base-case range (free, no ADR, deterministic) and an operator-typed thesis cannot tell the operator which bought the result, and the composed half is the one that costs nothing and works unattended. Second, circularity: the operator writes the sentence, then three blind judges score `view_stated` and `view_argued_not_recited` on it, and the operator knows the document is being measured. Every plan's anti-gaming clause covers discarding badly-reading runs; none covers authoring the measured field. AZN #2 already scored view_stated [true,true,true] and argued [true,true,true] with no operator involvement at all — the thesis section wrote it — and act was ['no','no','no'].
gaps.suggestedItem: Ship the composed half alone first (header carries the base-case range, the method and, once a price exists, the implied up/downside; `what_would_change_the_view` becomes required on the thesis contract) and judge one round on that. Only if it moves nothing is the judgement layer, its ADR and its 4–6 sessions worth buying. If the operator-authored view is built, pre-register it as a separate arm with one document carrying it and one not, and declare in the protocol that the authored field is excluded from the view_stated/argued targets.

gaps.what: No plan can measure, on the fake scene, the gate-page numbers three of them put in their ISSUE-1 exit criteria.
gaps.whyItMatters: Plans 2, 3 and 4 all claim ISSUE 1 is free because audit/smoke.py drives the whole workflow offline — which is true; it runs the fake scene through `drive(...)` against `StubSecClient` and the fake provider for £0. But the stub's aggregate is tests/fixtures/sec/companyfacts_msft.json at 4,506 bytes, against a real MSFT companyfacts artefact the judges describe as a multi-megabyte JSON, from which the run chose 18,610 facts and could not place 496 tags. So the fake scene's unmapped-concepts gate has a handful of rows. The targets 'the unmapped gate's first screen under twenty rows', 'the bank's gate-page total under 20,000 words' and 'fewer than twenty rows above the fold on the MSFT #1 payload' are not measurable on the instrument the plans specify.
gaps.suggestedItem: Split the ISSUE-1 harness in two, explicitly: shape assertions that survive a stub (forward control on every stopped state, zero UUIDs, zero CLI commands in visible text, approve control present) run on the fake scene; anything about page size, row counts or materiality banding is re-rendered against the committed gate payloads (gate-UNMAPPED_CONCEPTS.json and friends under docs/plan/readiness-audit-2026-09/*/). Both are free; they are different instruments and no plan says so.

gaps.what: Nobody read the console's own sources to find out what the platform must fetch. Three of four plans instead spend an operator decision and an ADR on the tier ceiling.
gaps.whyItMatters: The record answers the question directly and contradicts the framing all four plans inherited from §4.1. The console's winning answer to AZN's first focus question is built entirely on SEC-archived primaries: Farxiga $8,492m FY2025 from an 'AR extract on 6-K', Brilinta −38% from the same AR extract, Soliris US −28% to $1,092m from the FY2025 20-F, CVRM $12,764m and V&IT $846m at −12% and −26% CER from the H1 press release (azn2 sceptic's read of document B). Every one is an exhibit to, or the body of, a filing under an accession the platform already lists. The azn2 sceptic says it outright in the decisive field: 'a note that cannot locate product-level revenue or a patent schedule for a company that publishes both … has an acquisition problem, not an evidence problem. Six source documents, five of them one XBRL endpoint and a 20-F, is not a research base for this brief.' On MSFT the same shape: the console's segment table came from an EX-99.1 under the accession whose cover page the platform downloaded.
gaps.suggestedItem: Spend one sitting building the source-by-source map of both console notes: for each figure the judges named as decisive, record which document it came from and whether that document is under an accession the platform already lists. Publish it in the protocol. On the evidence so far it will show the entire measured gap closes with exhibit acquisition, content-aware current-report selection and Item 8 / Item 18 note excerpting — and that the T5 ceiling, its ADR against ADR 0092 and ADR 0111, its claim-level tier-marking precondition and the recent_developments section can all be cut from the first pass.

gaps.what: No plan has an abandonment criterion — a result that means stop spending and narrow the product's claim.
gaps.whyItMatters: Every plan has a measurement gate and every gate is phrased as 'if X does not move, re-plan'. None says what result would mean the platform should not try to beat a console note at all, and should instead be sold as what §4.3 already says it is good at: use case 10, 'Checking the work — yes, in the interface … This is the platform's strongest result, and it is the one the console cannot match.' That is a real possible outcome: the comparator is one API call at £6.71–£11.03 that a model upgrade improves for free, and the platform is 95 sessions of code at £7 a document. A plan with no stopping rule spends the whole estimate to find out.
gaps.suggestedItem: Pre-register one: if, after the first round, no comparison dimension has moved and no judge's stated reason has changed category, the programme stops at the completed workstreams, the product documentation narrows its claim to an auditable evidence base for SEC filers, and the remaining budget goes to the interface use case the audit already scores 'yes'. Write it into the protocol beside the targets, where it costs nothing and is honest; written after the result, it reads as a retreat.

gaps.what: No plan states the complete remaining checklist gap on the only post-fix document, and every plan therefore funds items the record shows are already closed.
gaps.whyItMatters: From the agreement block, azn2:platform scores present-sourced on: recent developments, capital allocation, key risks, regulatory/legal, a valuation with stated assumptions and a per-share result, and — decisively — 'a bear case with a number attached' [present-sourced ×3]. The complete remaining absent set is four rows: segment revenue, management guidance, management/board changes, competitive position with named competitors. The console's own absent set on azn2 is two: management/board changes and key risks. So the measured checklist gap is four rows against two, and one of them (management/board changes) the console fails too. Yet every plan funds the scenario engine as the fix for 'a bear case with a number attached', which azn2 already scores at the top.
gaps.suggestedItem: Write the four-row gap into the plan as the complete checklist scope and size only it: segment revenue (the dimensioned-facts carve-out), guidance (the results exhibit), named competitors (naming the confirmed peer set — an hour), and board changes (already reachable from the 8-K/6-K stream). Re-ground the scenario engine on msft1, where the row is absent 3/3, and drop its claim on azn2 entirely.

wrongAssumptions: That a stated view moves the verdict. The record shows it is necessary-sounding and unproven. AZN #2 scored view_stated [true,true,true] and argued [true,true,true] — the thesis section wrote it with no operator and no rating column — and would_act_on_it was ['no','no','no'] with all three comparisons still choosing the console. §4.1's own words: 'It changed no verdict.' Nothing in the record shows a document with a view beating one without it, holding anything else fixed. Every plan treats 'the view' as the first or second workstream on strength of judges' self-reported reasons, which is the weakest class of evidence in the file.

That the view the plans propose is the view the judges scored. What the console offered was 'UNDERWEIGHT | Target price $405 | Last close $493.16 | 12-month horizon' with expected total return −17.1% (msft1 operator, what_B_has_that_A_lacks). That is a rating, a target price and an expected return — four of the six strings in RESERVED_OUTPUT_FIELDS. All four plans correctly refuse a model-written version and then substitute an operator-typed judgement at gate 2, which fills the header column but is a different artefact, is unavailable on any unattended run, and — critically — is written by the same person whose satisfaction the round is measuring.

That peer multiples matter. The console has none either. Its own still_to_look_up lists 'Peer multiples for the ten companies listed as not sourced in Section 14' (azn, operator, doc B) and 'Peer multiples for Merck, Novartis, Roche, GSK, Sanofi, Pfizer, BMS, Lilly and Amgen — an Underweight resting solely on a DCF has no cross-check without them (§14)' (azn2, operator, doc B), and 'Peer data for AWS and Google Cloud … §17' (msft1, sceptic, doc B). The console won 51 of 54 dimension votes carrying a ten-row table of 'not sourced'. The measured checklist row is 'competitive position with named competitors', not 'peer multiple' — and the console scored present-*unsourced* on msft1 for two of three lenses, i.e. naming companies with no figures is enough to score present.

That the evidence policy is the blocker. The azn2 sceptic's decisive field says the opposite in as many words: 'has an acquisition problem, not an evidence problem'. The console's winning AZN answers came from an AR extract on a 6-K, the FY2025 20-F and the H1 press release; its winning MSFT segment table came from an EX-99.1 in an accession the platform opened. None of it is T5. Raising the ceiling would move the platform toward exactly what judges docked the console for — one CNBC sentence (msft1 sceptic), Dukascopy for the whole 30 June balance sheet (azn2 operator and sceptic), btw.media and a Substack (msft1 operator) — for no measured gain.

That the judges' per-dimension votes measure dimensions. Across nine comparisons and six dimensions, the 54 votes are console 51, equal 3, platform 0 — and all three 'equal' verdicts are on verifiability. Not one comparison split in the platform's favour on any dimension. A judge who prefers a document prefers it on everything. So the per-dimension scores carry no information independent of the headline, and every plan's per-dimension threshold ('verifiability ≥4 of 6', 'better_answers_the_brief ≥3 of 6') asks a measure that has never once deviated to deviate repeatedly.

That nine comparisons is the sample. Three of them (the azn round) judge a document whose valuation was withheld entirely by F-12, a bug already fixed — the platform would not ship that document today. The three lenses agreed on would_act_on_it 9 times of 9 and on every dimension bar three equals. So the effective independent sample for the current product is one document (azn2) read by three near-identical lenses. All four plans set 3-of-6 and 4-of-6 thresholds inside that noise.

That the export is where verifiability was lost, and that fixing it flips the vote. The sceptic who read azn2 wrote 'I did not prefer B on verifiability. A's provenance mechanism is better in kind' — and chose B anyway, scoring verifiability 'equal'. And the check-minutes gap is almost entirely msft1: platform [20,30,15] vs console [10,15,12] there, but azn2 platform [12,10,20] vs console [10,12,12] and azn platform [15,10,12] vs console [12,15,12]. On the post-fix document the platform is already at parity on checking time. Plan 1's acceptance ('≤10 in at least 2 of 3 reads') would be claimable today from noise on azn2.

That the console will stand still. It is three constants in audit/baseline/anthropic_baseline.py — MODEL 'claude-opus-5', EFFORT 'high', 25 searches — and src/aer/providers/costs.py already prices 'claude-fable-5-1' as 'The tier above Opus, which the provider already accepts as a route'. The comparator is already a tier behind on day one of the plan, improves for free, and §9 notes the baseline is the API and not the console a person would actually use.

That the judging is priced. §7: 'The judged reads and the code reading were paid for in this session's own tokens, not in pounds from the £100.' reads.json records no model, no effort and no prompt. Every plan's per-round judging figure (£2.50 a pair, £7.50, £21, £31.50) is an estimate of a number nobody measured for a configuration nobody recorded — and Plan 1 says so in its own open questions before putting the estimate in the headline total.

That reading length is the problem. Judges read the platform *faster*: 30–45 minutes against the console's 45–60, on documents of comparable size. The brief's premise about length is wrong, Plan 3 says so, and the other three still carry length-reduction items (footnote de-duplication, word-budget reallocation) as if they served ISSUE 2. They serve a reader; they do not serve the vote.
sequencingObjections: Every plan schedules the T5 tier-ceiling decision — an operator decision, a new ADR arguing against ADR 0092 and ADR 0111, claim-level tier marking as a precondition, and in three of four a nineteenth section. On the record it should be cut from the first pass entirely: the console's decisive material on both subjects came from SEC exhibits and filings the platform already has the accession for. Doing the ceiling before the acquisition work means the operator takes the plan's riskiest recorded-decision change to solve a problem the cheap deterministic work may already close, and then cannot tell which one worked.

Every plan attaches the scenario engine to 'a bear case with a number attached'. That checklist row is already present-sourced 3/3 on azn2 (agreement block), so the item cannot move the measure it is sold on. It is absent 3/3 on msft1 only. Either re-ground it on msft and drop its azn claim, or move it behind the four rows that are genuinely absent on azn2 (segment revenue, guidance, board changes, named competitors).

Plan 4's primary ISSUE-2 bar is 'better_on_verifiability names the platform in at least 4 of 6' — the single worst available choice. Verifiability is the only dimension where the instrument has ever produced anything other than a clean sweep (three 'equal' votes), the platform was already judged 'better in kind' there by the sceptic who chose the console anyway, and check-minutes on the post-fix document are already at parity. Plan 1 makes the same measure threshold 2 and Plan 3 threshold 1. If the instrument's per-dimension votes are a halo of the headline (they are: 51-3-0 with no split), none of these bars is reachable without an overall flip, and an overall flip makes them redundant.

Plan 3 spends fifteen sessions and the first £7.50 on instrument before one product defect is fixed, and its own risk register concedes an operator may ask what they bought. The defensible core of that choice is its step 4 — the calibration round, re-judging September's committed corpus with the coded panel and requiring it to reproduce the recorded verdict. That single idea is the best in any of the four plans and the other three omit it. But fifteen sessions is the wrong size: calibration plus the pre-registration is two or three sittings, and the metric promotions (filing_agreement's ruff/mypy migration of 1,284 exempted lines, the mutation corpus) belong after the first signal, not before it.

Plan 1's steer at step 7 is the cheapest early ISSUE-2 signal anyone proposes (£10.50, one AZN run, at ~19 sessions) and it is the right instinct. But it runs before Plan 1's own W8 dead-end inventory is measured and before the recovery work it labels 'programme prerequisite' has been proved live — on a product where three of six September runs did not reach an approved report. A single stranded steer costs the signal and the money. Move the harness and the two recovery actions ahead of it, which Plan 1 already schedules at step 2 and then does not wait for.

Plan 2 correctly puts the recovery work and the bank before any live spend and buys its first proof at step 4 for £8 — the best-sequenced live run in the four. But its first ISSUE-2 signal is step 9 at £11 after roughly 35 sessions, and its verdict round at step 15 after ~60. Between step 9 and step 15 it commits the tier ceiling, peer acquisition and the whole prose workstream on one mid-point read of re-rendered documents. That is a long unmeasured stretch for the most contested half of the plan.

All four plans commission MSFT twice inside a round and call the pair a free variance check while also judging one of them. §3.1 shows the pair differs by 5.6% on value per share because the operator confirmed 14× rather than 15×. Either the pair is a variance instrument (assumptions deliberately re-confirmed identically, and neither judged) or it is two judged documents (assumptions pinned by the protocol); it cannot be both, and no plan says which.

Three plans put the export/footnote-excerpt work before or alongside the acquisition work on the argument that it is the cheapest flip. Given the correlated-vote finding and the azn2 sceptic's 'better in kind … I did not prefer B on verifiability', the honest expectation is that it improves the document for a reader and moves no vote. It should be sequenced on its own merits — after the four absent checklist rows — not as the ISSUE-2 lever, and its exit criterion should be the reader-verifiability counts, not a comparison verdict.

Every plan writes the pre-registration and then schedules the roadmap rewrite separately (Plan 2 step 13, Plan 3 step 1, Plan 4 WS9). CLAUDE.md makes ROADMAP.md the authority on scope and both its live 'next' pointers name closed items. A plan that spends 40 sessions before its own items exist in the roadmap is a second authority for 40 sessions, which is precisely the condition that let §8's sixteen decisions sit unordered since the audit landed. It belongs in the first sitting in all four.
cheapestWinsMissed: Add two rubric keys — 'what one change to A would move you off no' and 'what would you need to see to prefer A' — and re-run the eighteen existing reads over the eighteen existing documents. Judge tokens only, no live run, no code. It converts a pile of complaints into a ranked backlog before ~40 sessions are spent on a guessed ranking, and it is the only cheap way to test whether 'the view' really is first.

Re-judge msft1 with the run console reachable, three reads. §4.1 concludes the verifiability advantage 'lives in the interface, not in the document it exports' and every one of the eighteen reads used report.md alone. If a judge with the interface still scores verifiability equal, the 5–7 session export workstream in every plan is buying a reader's convenience and not a vote — which is worth knowing for the price of three reads.

Name the eight operator-confirmed peers in §17 and in the industry section. An hour of deterministic prose over a gate payload the operator already approved; no ADR (ADR 0034 governs the withheld type's figures, not a company's name); no licence question. It is the only change that moves 'competitive position with named competitors' — absent 3/3 on msft1 and 3/3 on azn2, present on the console — and three of four plans bundle it behind the comps render work or an ADR amendment.

Stop printing 'Non-binding view: no view reached' where the run holds a base-case per-share figure, and print the composed range and method instead. One render branch at render/markdown.py, no ADR, no operator decision, no new field — assemble_document already takes `rating: str | None`. It removes the single most-quoted sentence in the judges' record (8 of 9 verdicts) months before the judgement-layer ADR lands. Plans 1 and 2 fold it into the view ADR and so cannot ship it early.

Re-render the committed gate payloads. gate-UNMAPPED_CONCEPTS.json exists for the audited runs; rendering the financials page against it is free and is the only honest measurement of the 7,911-word MSFT page and the 13,592-word bank page. Every plan promises to shrink those pages and every plan proposes to measure them on a fake scene whose companyfacts fixture is 4,506 bytes.

Map both console notes source-by-source, one sitting, no spend. For each figure the judges called decisive, record the document it came from and whether the platform's own submissions index already lists that accession. On the AZN evidence already in reads.json this will retire the tier-ceiling decision, its ADR and the recent_developments section from the first pass, and redirect the sessions to exhibit acquisition and note excerpting — which is a larger saving than any single item in any of the four plans.

Bound `_trim` to significant figures and replace the two hardcoded 'Recorded at this run's approval' strings. An hour. Today a shareable surface prints '169.798802002887 to 333.476013557285 USD/shares' and promises a view it never records — exactly the kind of thing the azn2 reader opened with. Every plan has it, buried mid-workstream; it should be in the first week because it costs nothing and is embarrassing.

Write the abandonment criterion into the pre-registration. Free, and it is the only line that makes the measurement gates real: without it, 'if X does not move, re-plan' means 'spend the next tranche and hope'. The honest candidate is already in §4.3 — use case 10 scores 'yes, in the interface' and is 'the one thing the console cannot do'.
